strengths: The framing of converting dense LLMs into MoE-style models via differentiable dynamic structural pruning without updating base weights is novel and interesting. The claim that experts 'inherently exist' inside dense MLP layers and can be exposed by routing/projection learning is a fresh perspective.

Empirical results are consistently strong across multiple model families (LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B, Phi-2) and multiple compression ratios, outperforming a wide set of baselines (SliceGPT, LLM-Pruner, ShortGPT, SLEB, LLM Surgeon, ModeGPT, DISP-LLM) on both perplexity and zero-shot tasks.

The design that differentiates static and dynamic pruning for MHA (top-K + static along the head dimension) versus top-1 routing for MLP experts is well-motivated and technically coherent; the RoPE/GQA compatibility discussion (Appendix A.2) is a thoughtful detail.

Overhead analysis is provided: trainable modules account for ~0.27% of parameters in LLaMA-2 7B, and training costs are reported to be comparable to or lower than DISP-LLM and much lower than LLM Surgeon.
Ablation studies on the regularization terms (R_P, R_U, load balancing), training diagnostics (loss curves), and expert-token visualizations add useful insight into the behavior of the method.
weaknesses: Despite the central motivation being efficiency ('fixed per-token budget', 'sparse and efficient computation'), no actual inference-time measurements are reported: no tokens/sec, latency, memory footprint, or FLOPs comparisons against baselines or the dense model. Without these, the efficiency claim - the primary selling point - is unsupported.

The 'MoE' framing is questionable: all experts share the same underlying W_G, W_U, W_D weights and are essentially different structured masks on a single MLP. This means total parameter storage/memory is not reduced; the method effectively performs input-dependent dynamic masking (closer to prior dynamic-pruning work than a true MoE). The paper does not clearly quantify or discuss end-to-end memory implications.

The absence of a direct comparison against the most relevant prior MoE-conversion baseline, LLaMA-MoE (Zhu et al., 2024), in the experiments is a significant omission. The related-work discussion alone cannot substitute for empirical comparison.

Several entries in Table 3 are missing ToMoE results (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B 70%, LLaMA-3 75%, and gaps in the Qwen table), which makes the reported apples-to-apples comparisons less complete and raises questions about table inconsistency.

It is unclear whether the widely reported 'pseudo-MoE' equivalence (Appendix B.3) actually yields runtime benefits; if experts can be materialized as a dense-like operation, this would strengthen the efficiency argument, but the paper does not verify any wall-clock speedup for either the MoE or the pseudo-MoE form.

The empirical gains over the most closely related method (DISP-LLM) are relatively modest at some ratios (e.g., 6.85 -> 6.41 ppl at 70% on LLaMA-2 7B), which raises the question of whether the improvement is worth the added architectural complexity of the MoE conversion.

Load-balancing loss oscillates around 0.15 (Section 4.4) rather than converging to a low value, which partially undermines the claim that the method achieves balanced expert loads; the token-routing visualizations also show inconsistent patterns (syntactic vs. semantic) across examples.

Reproducibility is not fully addressed: no statement about code or checkpoint release, and some training details (e.g., mixing-ratio sensitivity, temperature/bias tuning of ST-GS, the exact set of tokens used to estimate K) are only partially specified in the appendix.

strengths: Proposes a coherent differentiable formulation that turns MLP blocks into expert masks and MHA blocks into head-dimension masks via straight-through Gumbel-Sigmoid/Softmax, with routing, projection, and hypernetwork parameters jointly optimized (Eqs. 1–10).

A practically attractive property: the base model weights are frozen and only lightweight modules are trained (Sec. 3.5), so the conversion cost is reported to be comparable to structural pruning (Fig. 5b), and the auxiliary modules can largely be discarded after conversion (Appendix A.1; only ~0.27% extra parameters).

Reports consistent perplexity and zero-shot improvements over many structural-pruning and semi-structured baselines across LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, Phi-2, and Qwen-2.5 (Tables 1–3, 6, 7), and includes ablations on the loss terms and dataset choice (Fig. 6) plus some effort on practical details such as RoPE-compatible head pruning (Sec. A.2).
weaknesses: The central motivation is reducing both compute and memory (Abstract/Intro), but the method does not reduce memory: the regularizers deliberately push the union of experts to cover the full dense model (Eq. 7, Fig. 5a), so total parameters and storage are essentially unchanged from the dense model. The claimed benefit is therefore only in activated compute, yet no throughput, latency, FLOPs, or peak-memory measurements are ever reported — a serious omission for an efficiency paper that repeatedly claims 'efficient model serving' and 'consistent computational costs.'

The core comparison is not apples-to-apples. Baseline structural pruning (LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT, etc.) actually shrinks the model, while ToMoE keeps all parameters resident and only sparsely activates them. Comparing under 'active parameters' structurally favors MoE, since MoE can exploit a much larger total capacity at the same activation budget. The paper never reports the true parameter/memory budget of ToMoE (sum of expert widths relative to d_mid, overlap, and total stored parameters), nor whether experts overlap. In addition, baselines are given their standard (often fine-tuned) budgets while ToMoE trains only masks — a difference the paper treats as a pure advantage without a matched comparison.

The headline interpretive claim that 'MoEs inherently exist within dense models and can be uncovered without updating model weights' is weakly supported. The only evidence is qualitative routing visualizations (Tables 4, 8, 9) showing some syntactic locality; there is no quantitative measure of expert specialization (e.g., mutual information between experts and token types, ablation of routing vs. uniform selection, or comparison to random neuron subsets). Mechanistically, the procedure is a top-k subset-of-neurons approximation of the dense FFN distilled via KL to the frozen teacher; calling this 'discovering inherent experts' is an overclaim.

Limited originality. Splitting the FFN middle dimension into experts and routing tokens is what LLaMA-MoE and MoE-ification already do, and dynamic conditional computation via differentiable masks is the 'feature boosting and suppression' line the authors themselves cite (Gao et al., 2019). The incremental novelty is the combination with hypernetwork-generated masks and the no-fine-tuning regime, which is useful but modest.

Reproducibility and presentation problems. Reference years are frequently wrong (e.g., Vaswani et al. listed as 2024, Brown et al. 2020, Jang et al. 2023, Gao et al. 2024 for two different papers, SparseGPT cited as 2022), several figure/table captions are garbled or mis-ordered, and there are typos ('seme-structural'). Critically, the hyperparameter description contradicts the objective: p in Eq. 8 is defined as the active-parameter ratio in (0,1], but Appendix C states p = {0.6,0.5,0.4,0.3} for active ratios {40%,50%,60%,70%}, i.e., inverted. Empty/merged cells in Tables 3 and 6 (e.g., no ToMoE at 70% for LLaMA-2 7B; a malformed ToMoE row for LLaMA-2 13B at 50%) and missing baselines at several settings further complicate verification. No code is provided.

Inference behavior of the MoE is not analyzed: top-1 routing over irregularly selected neuron subsets implies gather/scatter over columns/rows of W_G, W_U, W_D, which typically hurts wall-clock speed despite lower FLOPs. The paper asserts consistent per-token cost but provides no evidence that the sparse implementation actually yields speedups, nor any expert-capacity/load-balance measurement at inference.
The Impact Statement claims decreased carbon emissions and broader access, which is not supported given that total parameters (and hence storage/memory) are not reduced.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper proposes a novel and useful angle for LLM compression: instead of permanently deleting parameters, it converts dense MLP/MHA layers into an MoE-style conditional computation model by learning routing/selection masks while keeping the base weights frozen. This connects dynamic structural pruning, MoE routing, and hypernetwork-based pruning in a coherent way.

Soundness/empirical support: The method is evaluated across several model families and scales, including LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B, and Phi-2, which is substantially broader than many pruning papers. The reported gains are consistent: e.g., ToMoE reaches 8.36 ppl at 50% active params on LLaMA-2 7B versus DISP-LLM 9.84, and 56.07 avg zero-shot accuracy versus 46.72 for DISP-LLM on LLaMA-2 7B at 50% active params.

The paper provides a detailed method design, including hypernetwork-generated expert embeddings, Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax/Sigmoid for differentiable discrete selection, union-of-experts regularization, parameter-budget regularization, and Switch-style load balancing. The ablation study gives useful insight into design choices: KL distillation is better than LM loss, union regularization matters more at aggressive pruning rates, and mixed WikiText/Alpaca/Code-Alpaca data improves performance.

Efficiency of training is partially supported: ToMoE's additional learned modules are small (reported 0.018B parameters for LLaMA-2 7B, about 0.27% overhead), and the paper reports training costs comparable to DISP-LLM and lower than LLM Surgeon. The use of in-place self-knowledge distillation avoids loading a separate teacher model, which is a practical advantage.

Reproducibility is reasonably good for a compression paper: implementation details such as optimizer, learning rate, batch size, GPU counts, hyperparameter settings, and module configurations are provided in the appendix, and experiments use public models and standard evaluation harnesses.

Presentation: The main idea and overall pipeline are clearly explained, with helpful figures showing static pruning, dynamic pruning, and the proposed MoE conversion. The training dynamics and width-allocation analyses add useful qualitative understanding.
weaknesses: The central efficiency motivation is not fully validated. The paper reports active parameter counts and training cost, but no wall-clock inference latency, throughput, memory footprint, or serving cost for the converted MoE. This is especially important because the proposed 'experts' are masked sub-networks of the original dense weights rather than separately stored experts; total memory may remain close to the dense model, and the practical serving gains of the MoE formulation are therefore unclear.

Comparison fairness needs clarification. ToMoE is trained on a mixed WikiText/Alpaca/Code-Alpaca dataset, while some baselines are evaluated without such mixed training or with different Alpaca variants. In Table 3, ToMoE results are missing for LLaMA-2 7B at 70% active parameters even though many baselines are shown there. It would be stronger to control training data, compute, and tuning budget across methods.

The claim that 'MoEs inherently exist within dense models and can be uncovered without updating model weights' is overstated. The base weights are frozen, but the router, projection, and hypernetwork parameters are trained for 10k iterations; without this learned routing/selection, no experts are uncovered. The finding is better framed as 'dense weights can be repurposed into conditional sub-networks via learned masks' rather than as latent experts existing a priori.

The converted model is not a standard MoE in the usual sense: different experts share the same underlying dense weight matrices and are defined by binary selection masks. This means the total parameter count is not reduced proportionally, and memory savings are not demonstrated. The terminology may confuse readers expecting separately parameterized experts or sparse MoE memory behavior.

Inference implementation details for MHA top-K routing are underexplored. Dynamic token-dependent selection along the head dimension may complicate efficient parallel prefilling and kernel implementation, even if all tokens use the same K. The paper asserts fixed computational cost but does not empirically validate it with real kernels or latency measurements.

Ablations are somewhat incomplete. The paper tests expert count N mainly on Qwen-2.5 and does not systematically study sensitivity to K in MHA, top-k choices, regularization weights alpha/beta/gamma, temperature, bias b, or random seeds. No variance or significance estimates are reported, making it hard to judge the robustness of the improvements.

Presentation and reproducibility have minor issues: there are several typos and naming inconsistencies (e.g., ModeGPT/MoDeGPT, 'seme-structural', 'Ob j.'), the main text omits some important implementation details that appear only in the appendix, and no code or released models are mentioned. A limitations section is also absent, though the impact statement is reasonable.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing: the paper connects dynamic structural pruning with Mixture-of-Experts construction, unifying expert construction and router training in a single stage rather than the two-stage pipelines of prior dense-to-MoE work (Zhang et al., Lee et al., Zhu et al.). The formulation as a differentiable dynamic pruning problem (Eq. 10) is clean and technically sound.

Strong and broad empirical evidence: consistent improvements over structural pruning and MoE-construction baselines are shown across Phi-2, LLaMA-2 (7B/13B), LLaMA-3 8B, and Qwen-2.5 (7B/14B), on both perplexity (Tab. 1-2) and a suite of zero/few-shot tasks (Tab. 3-6, 9-12). Improvements are large against most baselines (e.g., +16 to +19 points over SliceGPT/ShortGPT on LLaMA-3).

Practical efficiency: only ~0.27% additional parameters for LLaMA-2 7B (Appendix A.1), training cost comparable to DISP-LLM and much lower than LLM Surgeon (Fig. 6b), and competitive inference throughput (Tab. 15).

Comprehensive analysis and ablations: training dynamics of each regularizer (Fig. 3), ablation over loss terms, dataset mixture, temperature, embedding scope, and MHA design (Fig. 6c, Tab. 13), plus layer-wise width (Fig. 5), union-of-experts (Fig. 6a), and expert/token allocation visualizations (Tab. 7, 11, 14).
Reproducibility: code is released, and detailed implementation/hyperparameter settings (optimizer, learning rate, GPU counts, module configurations) are provided in Appendices A and C.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction claim the method works 'without requiring any weight updates' / 'without fine-tuning the model weights'. This is misleading: ToMoE trains a hypernetwork, routers, and per-layer projection modules for 10,000 iterations via knowledge distillation (Sec. 3.5, Sec. 4.1). While the original dense weights are frozen, this is still a non-trivial training procedure, and the framing overstates the distinction from fine-tuning.

The claim that ToMoE 'consistently outperforms ... MoE construction techniques' is contradicted by Tab. 6, where ToMoE (57.48 avg) underperforms LLaMA-MoE-v2 E8A2 (59.61) and E8A1S1 (59.31). The text softens this to 'comparable performance', but the headline claim in the abstract is not fully supported.

Comparison fairness is unclear. The token-count framing ('# Tokens: 0.02B' for ToMoE vs 1.2B/7B for LLaMA-MoE variants) is not directly comparable because ToMoE also trains auxiliary modules (hypernetwork/router/projections) for 10,000 iterations. Some baselines are evaluated with zero additional training while others are fine-tuned, and the '+fine-tuning' LLaMA-MoE row is trained for 'the same number of iterations as ToMoE', which conflates two very different training regimes.

The central interpretive claim that 'MoE inherently exists within dense models' is not rigorously demonstrated; the evidence (token-allocation visualizations in Tab. 7/11/14) is suggestive but qualitative, and the paper itself notes that 'further investigation is required'. This should be presented as a hypothesis rather than a finding.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (DISP-LLM) are sometimes modest (e.g., 1.48 perplexity points at 50% on LLaMA-2 7B), which weakens the strength of the 'obvious' performance-gap language used throughout.

Presentation problems: typos and errors such as 'Compassion against MoE construction methods' (Tab. 4 title), 'Poi et al., 2025' vs 'Pei et al., 2025', overlapping/garbled figure captions (Figs. 1-2), odd claims like 'ToMoE is 3.14 times better than ModeGPT', and a malformed Table 7/11/14 layout reduce clarity.
There is no dedicated limitations section, despite several design choices (top-1 MLP routing, head-dimension MHA pruning, single dataset mixture) that likely constrain applicability.

strengths: The method is clearly formulated mathematically: the unified conversion of MLP layers into top-1-routed experts via learned binary selection masks (Eq. 2-3) and of MHA layers into top-K/static head-dimension pruning (Eq. 4-5) is well specified, and the differentiable (Gumbel-Softmax/Sigmoid with straight-through) treatment of discrete routing/selection is coherent and implementable.

The empirical comparison against structural-pruning baselines is strong and broad. Tables 1-3 show ToMoE attaining lower perplexity than DISP-LLM, LLM Surgeon, ModeGPT, SliceGPT, etc. across LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B, and Qwen-2.5 7B/14B, sometimes beating baselines that retain more active parameters (e.g., 50% ToMoE = 8.36 vs DISP-LLM's 9.84 at 50%).

The resource profile is attractive: only ~0.02B training tokens and ~0.27% additional parameters for LLaMA-2 7B (Appendix A.1), with self-knowledge distillation avoiding extra model copies, and inference throughput shown to approach LLaMA-MoE (Table 15).

The design rationale is thoughtfully supported by targeted ablations and analysis: regularization choices (R_U, R_P, R_L), the RoPE-compatible handling of head-dimension pruning (A.2), the justification for static Q/K pruning vs. dynamic V/O pruning (Appendix F), and temperature sensitivity (Table 13).
weaknesses: A central claim is contradicted by the paper's own data. The text in Sec. 4.3 states ToMoE 'consistently surpasses all baselines' and the abstract claims it 'consistently outperforms... MoE techniques,' yet Table 6 shows ToMoE averaging 57.48 versus LLaMA-MoE-v2 E8A2 at 59.61 and E8A1S1 at 59.31. ToMoE is lower on the average and on most subtasks (BoolQ 63.67 vs 74.62/76.88; ARC-C 37.29 vs 42.83/40.19; MMLU 36.31 vs 37.41/40.89). The 'consistently surpasses' framing is therefore unsupported.

The headline conceptual claim that 'MoE inherently exists within dense models' and can be 'uncovered without updating model weights' is overstated. Routers, projection modules, the hypernetwork, and the expert selection masks are all learned, and the mask for an expert can span the entire MLP intermediate dimension, so this is better described as learning to construct experts than as revealing pre-existing ones. The 'self-knowledge distillation with frozen weights' only avoids updating the base MLP/attention weights, not the substantial learned machinery that defines the experts.

The expert-specialization visualizations do not support the analysis they are meant to motivate. Tables 7, 11, and 14 purport to show token-to-expert allocation, but the content is identical (or in Table 7, an unformatted string prefixed with '@>') across all experts/layers, conveying no visible differentiation. Likewise the claim in Sec. 4.4/Tab. 7 that 'each expert aligns syntax rather than semantic meanings' is not substantiated by the shown rendering.

Comparison fairness is questionable. The '# Tokens' column pits ToMoE's 0.02B (router-only training, ~10k iterations) against 1.2B/7B for baselines that perform continual pre-training of full model weights (LLaMA-MoE, LLaMA-MoE-v2, CMoE). Mixing router-only training with full-weight pre-training in the same table conflates two different regimes, and the claimed 'significantly fewer tokens' advantage follows partly from not training the weights at all.

Originality is limited. The pipeline (hypernetwork-generated pruning embeddings, ST-Gumbel masks, regularization on active parameters/union) closely follows DISP-LLM (Gao et al., 2024), which is acknowledged. The incremental step is to reinterpret the learned masks as experts with top-1 routing; the paper does not isolate which technical ingredient drives the gains relative to DISP-LLM.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: multiple copy-edit errors and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Compassion against MoE construction methods' in Table 4; 'Poi et al., 2025' vs 'Pei et al., 2025'; 'ModeGPT' vs 'MoDeGPT'; several references with mismatched years, e.g., Gao et al., Ma et al., Touvron et al.). The promised code link is blank in the manuscript, weakening reproducibility for a method whose exact masking/projection details are non-trivial.

strengths: The paper introduces a unified approach to convert dense LLMs into Mixture-of-Experts models via dynamic structural pruning, without updating the original model weights. The method trains only small routing/projection/hypernetwork modules (about 0.27% extra parameters), making it efficient and practical.

Empirical results are strong and cover multiple models (Phi-2, LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-2.5) and tasks. ToMoE consistently outperforms structured pruning baselines such as LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT, DISP-LLM, and MoE construction baselines in most reported settings, often with much fewer training tokens (e.g., 0.02B vs. 1.2B/7B in Table 5).

The paper provides detailed analysis: training dynamics, layer-wise width allocation, router behavior, expert token allocation, and ablations over design choices (knowledge distillation, union regularization, dataset mixture, temperature). This helps understand the method and supports the design.

Presentation is clear and well structured, with informative figures and a detailed appendix covering module configurations, RoPE compatibility, Gumbel-Softmax/Sigmoid details, and additional experiments (throughput, more models). Reproducibility is reasonably supported despite some missing details.

The conversion enables a fixed expected per-token budget and retains compatibility with standard MoE system support, which is a meaningful step for deploying compressed LLMs with conditional computation.
weaknesses: The central claim that 'MoE inherently exists within dense models' and can be 'uncovered without updating weights' is not rigorously established. The method effectively learns a structured decomposition via masks; the visualizations show some semantic specialization, but there is no quantitative or causal evidence that the experts pre-exist rather than being learned by the router/mask optimization.

The abstract and introduction claim ToMoE 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art pruning and MoE techniques,' but Table 6 contradicts this for LLaMA-3 8B at 50% active parameters: ToMoE average 57.48 is lower than LLaMA-MoE-v2 E8A2 (59.61) and E8A1S1 (59.31). The paper should tone down or contextualize this claim.

Comparisons focus on active parameter count, but ToMoE retains all experts and thus total storage/memory is roughly dense (plus small router overhead). Static pruning methods reduce total parameter count. The paper does not discuss this total-memory trade-off or compare memory/storage footprint, which is critical for deployment.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no repeated runs, seeds, error bars, or significance tests. Most results are single numbers, which may not be robust. Some tables also use inconsistent active-parameter terminology (e.g., '60%' in Table 1 vs. Table 3), making cross-table comparison harder.

The method builds heavily on DISP-LLM's hypernetwork-based dynamic structural pruning; the technical novelty relative to that work is moderate, and the paper could better clarify what is genuinely new beyond MoE routing and regularizations.

Ablation results show that dynamic MHA routing (VO routing) contributes only about 1% improvement, raising questions about its necessity. The core benefit appears to come mainly from MLP expert conversion, which is not sufficiently disentangled.

There is no dedicated limitations or broader-impact discussion. The paper does not discuss failure cases, memory constraints, potential biases inherited from dense models, or deployment scenarios where total memory rather than active compute is the bottleneck. The code URL is also missing from the abstract.
